denominations.name: Traditional and folk religions
denominations.text: Local ancestral, animist and nature religions, passed on orally rather than through a scripture or church.

history.title: Ancestral faiths everywhere
history.text: In c. 4000 BC nearly every people on earth followed local animist, ancestral and nature religions, from the farmers of Africa, Europe and Asia to the hunters of the Americas and Australia.

history.title: First state religions emerge
history.text: From c. 3000 BC the local cults of Egypt, Mesopotamia, India and China grew into organised state religions with priests, temples and writing, while most of the world kept its oral traditions.

history.title: Axial Age faiths spread
history.text: From c. 500 BC Buddhism, Jainism, Confucianism and Zoroastrianism began to replace or absorb local traditions across Asia, though village and ancestor cults lived on beneath them.

history.title: Christianity and Islam advance
history.text: After Rome adopted Christianity and the Arab conquests began in 632, the two faiths spread through Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, shrinking the lands of traditional religion.

history.title: Sahel kings adopt Islam
history.text: In the 11th century the rulers of Takrur and Kanem converted to Islam through trans-Saharan trade, beginning the slow Islamization of West African elites while most farmers kept their own gods.

history.title: Conquest of the Americas
history.text: After 1492 Spanish and Portuguese conquest and missions Christianized most of the Americas, and later Russian expansion did the same in much of Siberia.

history.title: Pacific islands convert
history.text: From c. 1820 Protestant missionaries converted Hawaii, Tahiti, Tonga, Fiji and Samoa, often after their chiefs or kings adopted Christianity, ending traditional religion as the majority faith across Polynesia.

history.title: Missions in colonial Africa
history.text: After the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, colonial rule and missionaries spread Christianity and Islam across sub-Saharan Africa, where most people still followed traditional religion in 1900.

history.title: Living traditions today
history.text: Few countries now have a traditional-religion majority, but ancestral and spirit beliefs survive across Africa, Siberia, the Americas, Oceania and Southeast Asia, often blended with Christianity or Islam.

denominations.name: Tengrism
denominations.text: The sky-god religion of the Turkic and Mongol steppe peoples, with shamans as intermediaries.

history.title: Xiongnu sons of Heaven
history.text: In 209 BC Modu Chanyu united the Xiongnu of the Mongolian steppe, whose rulers were styled sons of Tengri, the Heaven god, according to Chinese records.

history.title: Gokturk Khaganate rises
history.text: In 552 the Gokturks founded a steppe empire from Manchuria to the Black Sea; their Orkhon inscriptions of the 730s credit Tengri and the earth goddess Umay with the khagans' power.

history.title: Uyghurs turn Manichaean
history.text: In 762 the Uyghur khagan Bogu adopted Manichaeism as state religion, the first great steppe power to set aside Tengri worship as its official cult.

history.title: Western Turks embrace Islam
history.text: Volga Bulgaria accepted Islam in 922 and the Karakhanids in the mid 10th century, beginning the conversion of the western and Central Asian Turks, including the Seljuks.

history.title: Genghis Khan's Eternal Heaven
history.text: In 1206 Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan; the Mongol Empire claimed to rule all lands under the mandate of Mongke Tengri, the Eternal Blue Heaven, while tolerating other faiths.

history.title: Mongol khanates convert
history.text: Ghazan made the Ilkhanate Muslim in 1295 and Uzbek Khan did the same for the Golden Horde from 1313, while the Yuan court in China favoured Tibetan Buddhism.

history.title: Mongols adopt Tibetan Buddhism
history.text: In 1578 Altan Khan met the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso and gave him the title Dalai Lama; the Mongols turned to Buddhism and shamanism was pushed to the margins.

history.title: Post-Soviet revival
history.text: Since the fall of the USSR in 1991, Tengrist and shamanic movements have revived in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Buryatia, Tuva, Altai and Yakutia, mostly as minority and cultural traditions.

denominations.name: Ancient Egyptian religion
denominations.text: The gods of the Nile with the pharaoh as divine king, centred on temples and the afterlife.

history.title: Egypt united under pharaoh
history.text: In c. 3100 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were united under the first kings, who ruled as divine intermediaries identified with the falcon god Horus.

history.title: Pyramids of Giza
history.text: In c. 2560 BC Khufu built the Great Pyramid at Giza, the height of the Old Kingdom royal cult tied to the sun god Ra and the king's afterlife.

history.title: New Kingdom and Amun
history.text: In c. 1550 BC Ahmose expelled the Hyksos; under the New Kingdom Amun-Ra of Thebes became the empire's chief god, and Egyptian temples spread into Nubia and Canaan.

history.title: Akhenaten's Aten revolution
history.text: In c. 1350 BC Akhenaten replaced the traditional gods with worship of the sun disc Aten at his new capital Amarna; the old cults were restored soon after his death.

history.title: Kushite pharaohs from Nubia
history.text: In c. 730 BC Piye of Kush, a devotee of Amun, conquered Egypt; Nubian kings at Napata and later Meroe kept Egyptian-style religion until the 4th century AD.

history.title: Alexander and the Ptolemies
history.text: In 332 BC Alexander took Egypt and was hailed son of Amun at Siwa; the Ptolemaic kings built temples such as Edfu and spread the cults of Isis and Serapis through the Greek world.

history.title: Roman Egypt, Isis abroad
history.text: After 30 BC Egypt became a Roman province; its temples kept working under emperors portrayed as pharaohs, and Isis worship spread as far as Rome, Gaul and Britain.

history.title: Theodosius closes the temples
history.text: In 391 Theodosius I banned pagan sacrifice and the Serapeum of Alexandria was destroyed; Egypt soon became overwhelmingly Christian.

history.title: Philae, the last temple
history.text: In c. 537 Justinian closed the temple of Isis at Philae, long kept open for Nubian worshippers, ending the last public cult of ancient Egyptian religion.

denominations.name: Mesopotamian and Canaanite religion
denominations.text: The city gods of Sumer, Babylon and Assyria and the related Canaanite and Phoenician cults of Baal and Astarte.

history.title: Sumerian temple cities
history.text: From c. 3500 BC Uruk and other Sumerian cities built great temples to gods such as An and Inanna, each city governed in the name of its patron deity.

history.title: Sargon of Akkad
history.text: In c. 2334 BC Sargon united Mesopotamia in the first empire; his daughter Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur, wrote the earliest hymns known by author.

history.title: Hammurabi and Marduk
history.text: In c. 1754 BC Hammurabi of Babylon issued his law code under the sun god Shamash, and Marduk of Babylon rose toward the head of the pantheon.

history.title: Canaanite gods at Ugarit
history.text: In c. 1400 to 1200 BC the tablets of Ugarit on the Syrian coast recorded the myths of El, Baal and Anat, the gods shared by the Canaanite city states.

history.title: Phoenicians carry Baal west
history.text: Tyre founded Carthage in c. 814 BC, and Phoenician traders spread the cults of Baal, Astarte and Melqart to Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia, North Africa and Spain.

history.title: Assyria wars for Ashur
history.text: In c. 700 BC the Assyrian empire, waging war in the name of its god Ashur, ruled from Egypt to western Iran, and Ashurbanipal's Nineveh library gathered its religious texts.

history.title: Persia takes Babylon
history.text: In 539 BC Cyrus the Great captured Babylon; Marduk's temple kept working under Persian and then Seleucid rule, but the old religion lost its royal patrons.

history.title: Rome destroys Carthage
history.text: In 146 BC Rome destroyed Carthage, though the Punic gods Baal Hammon and Tanit lived on in Roman Africa under the names Saturn and Caelestis.

history.title: Last cuneiform tablet
history.text: The last datable cuneiform astronomical tablet from Babylon dates to c. AD 75, marking the fading of the old Mesopotamian temple culture.

history.title: Theodosius bans sacrifice
history.text: In 391 Theodosius I banned pagan sacrifice, ending the public cults of Baal and Astarte in Roman Syria and Phoenicia; only small pockets, such as the moon cult of Harran, lingered on.

denominations.name: Greek and Roman religion
denominations.text: The Olympian gods of Greece and Rome, worshipped through civic temples, sacrifice and oracles, with the Roman emperor cult added later.

history.title: Mycenaean gods
history.text: By c. 1200 BC the Mycenaean palaces of Greece recorded offerings to Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus on Linear B tablets.

history.title: First Olympic Games
history.text: In 776 BC, by tradition, the first games for Zeus were held at Olympia; Homer and Hesiod soon fixed the family of Olympian gods shared by all Greeks.

history.title: Colonies spread Greek gods
history.text: From c. 750 BC Greek colonies carried temples and oracles from Spain and Sicily to the Black Sea, while Rome and the Etruscans adopted many Greek gods under Latin names.

history.title: Parthenon of Athens
history.text: In 447 BC Athens began the Parthenon for its patron Athena, a high point of classical civic religion alongside Delphi's oracle and the Eleusinian Mysteries.

history.title: Alexander's Hellenistic world
history.text: In 334 BC Alexander invaded Persia; his successors planted Greek cults and temples from Egypt and Syria to Bactria, blending them with local gods.

history.title: Augustus and emperor cult
history.text: In 27 BC Augustus became the first Roman emperor; worship of Roma and the deified emperors joined the old gods across an empire from Britain to Syria.

history.title: Constantine turns Christian
history.text: In 312 Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge under a Christian sign, and the Edict of Milan in 313 began the shift of imperial favour from the old gods to Christianity.

history.title: Julian's pagan revival
history.text: From 361 to 363 Emperor Julian tried to restore temple sacrifice and organise paganism like a church, but his revival ended with his death in Persia.

history.title: Theodosius bans sacrifice
history.text: In 391 and 392 Theodosius I banned pagan sacrifice and temple worship throughout the empire, and the Olympic Games ended soon after.

history.title: Justinian closes the Academy
history.text: In 529 Justinian barred pagans from teaching, ending the Platonic Academy of Athens; the last rural pockets, such as the Mani peninsula, converted by the 9th century.

denominations.name: Celtic, Germanic, Norse and Slavic paganism
denominations.text: The pre-Christian religions of northern and eastern Europe: druids, Odin and Thor, Perun and the Baltic gods.

history.title: Celtic world and druids
history.text: From c. 450 BC the La Tene Celts spread from Gaul to Bohemia and Iberia, led by druid priests who worshipped at sacred groves, springs and lakes.

history.title: Caesar conquers Gaul
history.text: By 52 BC Caesar had conquered Gaul, where Celtic gods merged with Roman ones; Rome later suppressed the druids, storming their stronghold on Anglesey in AD 60.

history.title: Clovis baptised
history.text: In c. 496 Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptised a Catholic, starting the conversion of the Germanic peoples who had settled in Gaul.

history.title: Mission to the Anglo-Saxons
history.text: In 597 Augustine landed in Kent to convert the pagan Anglo-Saxons; with Irish monks from the north, England was Christian by c. 690.

history.title: Charlemagne fells Irminsul
history.text: In 772 Charlemagne destroyed the Saxon sacred pillar Irminsul and began a 30-year war that forced the Saxons to accept Christianity.

history.title: Baptism of the Rus
history.text: Vladimir of Kiev was baptised in 988, after Mieszko of Poland in 966 and before Iceland's vote for Christianity in 1000, shrinking pagan Europe to Scandinavia and the Baltic.

history.title: Scandinavia becomes Christian
history.text: By c. 1100 Scandinavia was Christian, after Olaf II's conversion of Norway and the end of the royal temple cult at Uppsala in Sweden.

history.title: Northern Crusades in Baltic
history.text: From 1230 the Teutonic Knights conquered the pagan Prussians, as German crusaders had done with the Livonians and Estonians, converting the Baltic coast by force.

history.title: Lithuania, last pagan state
history.text: In 1387 Lithuania, Europe's last pagan state, was officially baptised after its grand duke Jogaila became king of Poland; Samogitia followed in 1413.

history.title: Modern pagan revival
history.text: In 1973 Iceland recognised the Asatru Fellowship, part of a small modern revival of Norse, Baltic, Slavic and Celtic paganism across Europe.

denominations.name: Mesoamerican religion
denominations.text: The temple-pyramid religions of the Olmec, Maya, Toltec and Aztec, with a shared calendar and gods like Quetzalcoatl.

history.title: Olmec ceremonial centres
history.text: From c. 1200 BC the Olmec of the Gulf Coast built ceremonial centres such as San Lorenzo, with were-jaguar gods, the sacred ballgame and colossal heads of their rulers.

history.title: Zapotecs and the calendar
history.text: In c. 500 BC the Zapotecs founded Monte Alban in Oaxaca, where some of the earliest glyphs of the 260-day ritual calendar shared across Mesoamerica appear.

history.title: Teotihuacan's great pyramids
history.text: In c. AD 100 to 250 Teotihuacan raised the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and the Feathered Serpent temple, making it the religious capital of central Mexico.

history.title: Classic Maya divine kings
history.text: From c. 250 the divine kings of Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan ruled through temple-pyramids, bloodletting rites and the Long Count calendar.

history.title: Maya collapse, Toltecs rise
history.text: In c. 900 the southern Maya cities were abandoned, while Toltec Tula and Chichen Itza spread the cult of the feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl, or Kukulcan.

history.title: Aztecs found Tenochtitlan
history.text: In 1325 the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan; from 1428 their Triple Alliance empire honoured Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc at the Templo Mayor with mass human sacrifice.

history.title: Spanish conquest of Mexico
history.text: In 1521 Cortes and his native allies took Tenochtitlan; temples were destroyed and Franciscan and Dominican friars converted central Mexico to Catholicism.

history.title: Fall of the last Maya kingdom
history.text: In 1697 Spain conquered Nojpeten in the Peten, the last independent Maya kingdom, ending Mesoamerican religion as a state faith.

history.title: Traditions within Catholicism
history.text: Today Maya and Nahua rites survive inside Catholic practice, and highland Guatemalan day-keepers still follow the 260-day calendar.

denominations.name: Andean religion
denominations.text: The religions of Chavin, Moche, Tiwanaku and the Inca, centred on the sun god Inti, mountain spirits and ancestor mummies.

history.title: Caral's sacred mounds
history.text: By c. 2500 BC Caral and other Norte Chico towns on the Peruvian coast built platform mounds and sunken plazas for communal rituals, the oldest monumental religion in the Americas.

history.title: Chavin cult spreads
history.text: From c. 900 BC the temple of Chavin de Huantar drew pilgrims, and its staff god and feline imagery spread across the highlands and coast of Peru.

history.title: Moche and Nazca
history.text: From c. AD 100 the Moche built the Huacas of the Sun and Moon on Peru's north coast, while the Nazca drew giant ritual lines and figures in the southern desert.

history.title: Tiwanaku and Wari
history.text: In c. 600 Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca, with its Gate of the Sun, and the Wari empire of the central highlands spread a shared staff god across the Andes.

history.title: Inca empire of Inti
history.text: From 1438 Pachacuti built the Inca empire, centred on the sun god Inti at Cusco's Coricancha, and imposed the sun cult and royal mummy worship from Ecuador to Chile.

history.title: Spanish conquest of Peru
history.text: In 1532 Pizarro captured the Inca Atahualpa at Cajamarca; the Spanish destroyed temples and huacas and began converting the Andes to Catholicism.

history.title: Fall of Vilcabamba
history.text: In 1572 the Spanish executed Tupac Amaru, last Inca of Vilcabamba; campaigns to extirpate idolatry from 1610 drove the old cults into hiding.

history.title: Inti Raymi revived
history.text: In 1944 Cusco revived the Inca sun festival Inti Raymi; today Quechua and Aymara offerings to Pachamama and the mountain apus continue alongside Catholicism.

denominations.name: Judaism
denominations.text: The monotheism of the Israelites, centred on the Torah, first on the Jerusalem Temple and after AD 70 on rabbis and synagogues.

history.title: Kingdom of David, c. 1000 BC
history.text: According to the Bible, David made Jerusalem the capital of Israel and his son Solomon built the First Temple there, centring the worship of the God of Israel.

history.title: Fall of Israel
history.text: Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and deported much of its people, leaving the southern kingdom of Judah as the heart of the faith.

history.title: Babylonian exile
history.text: Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple and exiled the elite to Babylon, where much of the Hebrew Bible took shape.

history.title: Return and Second Temple
history.text: Cyrus the Great of Persia allowed exiles to return, and the Second Temple was completed around 516 BC.

history.title: Maccabean revolt
history.text: The Maccabees rebelled against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV and rededicated the Temple in 164 BC, later ruling an independent Jewish kingdom.

history.title: Destruction of the Temple
history.text: The Romans destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70 and crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135, so Judaism became a diaspora faith led by rabbis, synagogues and the Talmud.

history.title: Khazar conversion, c. 740
history.text: The ruling elite of the Khazar khaganate north of the Caucasus adopted Judaism, the only large state with Jewish rulers between antiquity and modern times.

history.title: Expulsion from Spain
history.text: Spain expelled its Jews in 1492 and Portugal in 1497; many found refuge in the Ottoman Empire, while Poland-Lithuania became the main centre of European Jewry.

history.title: The Holocaust
history.text: Nazi Germany and its allies murdered about six million Jews from 1941 to 1945, destroying the great Jewish communities of eastern and central Europe.

history.title: State of Israel
history.text: Israel was founded in 1948 and Jews from the Middle East and Europe moved there; today about 15 million Jews live mostly in Israel and the United States.

denominations.name: Zoroastrianism
denominations.text: Zarathustra's faith in the wise lord Ahura Mazda and the struggle of good against evil, state religion of three Persian empires.

history.title: Zarathustra's Gathas
history.text: In c. 1200 BC (estimates range from 1500 to 600 BC) Zarathustra composed the Gathas in eastern Iran, preaching the wise lord Ahura Mazda against the lie and its demons.

history.title: Darius and Ahura Mazda
history.text: From 522 BC Darius I credited his rule to Ahura Mazda in royal inscriptions, as the Achaemenid empire stretched from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus.

history.title: Alexander burns Persepolis
history.text: In 330 BC Alexander destroyed the Achaemenid empire and burned Persepolis; under Seleucid and then Parthian rule Zoroastrianism coexisted with Greek cults.

history.title: Sasanian state church
history.text: In 224 Ardashir I founded the Sasanian empire, which made Zoroastrianism a state church with fire temples, a powerful priesthood and an organised Avesta canon.

history.title: Arab conquest of Iran
history.text: The last Sasanian shah Yazdegerd III died in 651 after the Arab conquest; Iran's population turned slowly to Islam and was mostly Muslim by c. 1000.

history.title: Parsis settle in Gujarat
history.text: Zoroastrians seeking refuge landed at Sanjan in Gujarat, traditionally c. 936 (some say 716), founding the Parsi community of India.

history.title: Jizya lifted in Iran
history.text: In 1882, after campaigns funded by Bombay Parsis, the Qajar shah abolished the jizya poll tax on Iran's dwindling Zoroastrians of Yazd and Kerman.

history.title: Small community today
history.text: Today perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 Zoroastrians remain, mainly in Mumbai, Yazd and Tehran and in diaspora communities in North America and Britain.

denominations.name: Manichaeism
denominations.text: Mani's dualist religion of light and darkness, which spread from Persia to Rome and China and was state religion of the Uyghurs.

history.title: Mani's revelation
history.text: In c. 240 Mani began preaching in Sasanian Mesopotamia a religion of light against darkness, uniting ideas from Zoroaster, Buddha and Jesus with its own scriptures.

history.title: Mani dies in prison
history.text: Mani died in prison in c. 276 under Bahram I, urged on by the Zoroastrian high priest Kartir; persecution scattered his followers west into Rome and east into Central Asia.

history.title: Diocletian's edict
history.text: In c. 302 Diocletian outlawed Manichaeism, yet it spread through Roman Egypt, Africa and Italy, where the young Augustine was a Manichaean hearer for nine years.

history.title: Mission to Tang China
history.text: In 694 a Manichaean missionary presented the faith's scripture at the Tang court, after Sogdian merchants had carried it along the Silk Road.

history.title: Uyghur state religion
history.text: In 762 the Uyghur khagan Bogu converted, making Manichaeism the state religion of the Uyghur empire on the Mongolian steppe.

history.title: Tang persecution
history.text: In 843, after the Uyghur empire fell, the Tang banned Manichaeism and killed many of its clergy in China.

history.title: Qocho turns Buddhist
history.text: The Uyghur kingdom of Qocho in Turfan kept Manichaean monasteries until Buddhism prevailed there in c. 1000, ending its last royal patronage.

history.title: Last shrine in Fujian
history.text: The Cao'an temple near Quanzhou in Fujian holds a Mani statue dated 1339; the faith survived there as the Religion of Light into the Ming era, then vanished.

denominations.name: Vedic religion
denominations.text: The fire sacrifices and hymns of the Vedas, the root of Hinduism.

history.title: Rigvedic hymns
history.text: In c. 1500 to 1200 BC Indo-Aryan tribes in the Punjab composed the Rigveda, hymns to Indra, Agni and Soma sung at fire sacrifices.

history.title: Kuru ritual and eastward spread
history.text: In c. 1000 BC the Kuru kingdom codified the great fire rituals in the Yajurveda and Brahmanas, and Vedic culture spread east into the Ganges plain.

history.title: The early Upanishads
history.text: From c. 700 BC the early Upanishads taught karma, rebirth and the unity of the self with brahman, turning Vedic thought inward.

history.title: Sramana challenge
history.text: In c. 500 BC the Buddha and Mahavira rejected Vedic sacrifice and brahmin authority, winning royal patrons in Magadha.

history.title: Shunga revival
history.text: In c. 185 BC Pushyamitra Shunga overthrew the Mauryas and revived the royal horse sacrifice, a brief return of Vedic kingship.

history.title: Absorbed into Hinduism
history.text: By the Gupta era from 320, temple worship of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess had largely replaced Vedic sacrifice, though the Vedas remained Hinduism's sacred root.

history.title: Living Vedic rites
history.text: In 1975 Nambudiri brahmins of Kerala performed the 12-day Athirathram fire ritual, one of the few places where ancient Vedic rites and chanting still survive.

denominations.name: Hinduism
denominations.text: The family of traditions devoted to Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess, built on the Vedas, the epics and temple worship.

history.title: Epics and devotion
history.text: From c. 500 BC the Mahabharata, with its Bhagavad Gita, and the Ramayana took shape, centring worship on Krishna, Rama and Shiva rather than Vedic sacrifice.

history.title: Gupta golden age
history.text: From 320 the Gupta kings patronised Vishnu and Shiva, the Puranas were compiled and the first stone temples rose, as Hinduism overtook Buddhism in royal favour.

history.title: Indianized Southeast Asia
history.text: From c. 400 Hindu kingdoms such as Funan, Champa and Tarumanagara in Java adopted Shiva and Vishnu worship and Sanskrit, carried by traders and brahmins.

history.title: Shankara and bhakti saints
history.text: In c. 800 Adi Shankara taught Advaita Vedanta and founded monasteries, while Tamil bhakti poets spread devotion to Shiva and Vishnu, helping Hinduism eclipse Buddhism in India.

history.title: Angkor Wat for Vishnu
history.text: From c. 1113 Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat for Vishnu, the high point of Hinduism in Southeast Asia before Cambodia turned to Theravada Buddhism.

history.title: Delhi Sultanate
history.text: In 1206 the Delhi Sultanate began centuries of Muslim rule over north India, but Hindus remained the majority, and the Vijayanagara empire from 1336 championed Hinduism in the south.

history.title: Majapahit falls, Bali remains
history.text: In c. 1527 the Hindu Majapahit kingdom of Java fell to Muslim Demak; Java became Muslim, but Bali kept its Hindu religion to this day.

history.title: Shivaji's Maratha kingdom
history.text: In 1674 Shivaji was crowned Hindu king of the Marathas, whose power came to dominate much of India in the 18th century as Mughal rule declined.

history.title: Independence and Partition
history.text: In 1947 India became independent as a secular republic with a Hindu majority, while Partition drove millions of Hindus out of the new Pakistan.

history.title: Third largest religion
history.text: Today about 1.2 billion Hindus form majorities in India and Nepal and on Bali, with large communities in Mauritius, Fiji, Britain and North America.

denominations.name: Jainism
denominations.text: Mahavira's path of non-violence and asceticism.

history.title: Mahavira's teaching
history.text: In c. 500 BC (traditional dates 599 to 527 BC) Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara, taught strict non-violence and asceticism in the kingdoms of Bihar.

history.title: Chandragupta goes south
history.text: By tradition, in c. 300 BC the Maurya emperor Chandragupta became a monk and followed the sage Bhadrabahu to Shravanabelagola, carrying Jainism into Karnataka.

history.title: Digambara and Svetambara split
history.text: The community divided into the sky-clad Digambaras and the white-clad Svetambaras, a split traditionally dated to AD 79 or 82.

history.title: Council of Valabhi
history.text: In c. 454 the Svetambara council at Valabhi in Gujarat wrote down its scriptural canon under the monk Devarddhi.

history.title: Gommateshwara statue
history.text: In c. 983 the minister Chavundaraya raised the 17 metre statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, at the height of royal Jain patronage in the Deccan.

history.title: Kumarapala in Gujarat
history.text: From 1143 King Kumarapala of Gujarat, guided by the monk Hemachandra, protected Jainism and banned animal slaughter, making Gujarat and Rajasthan its lasting heartland.

history.title: Small but influential today
history.text: India's 2011 census counted about 4.5 million Jains, mainly in Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Karnataka, with diaspora communities in Britain, North America and East Africa.

denominations.name: Early Buddhism
denominations.text: The Buddha's teaching in its first Indian centuries, before the Theravada and Mahayana traditions separated.

history.title: The Buddha's awakening
history.text: In c. 500 BC (dates range from 563 to 400 BC) Siddhartha Gautama attained awakening at Bodh Gaya and taught the Middle Way in the Ganges kingdoms of Magadha and Kosala.

history.title: Second council and schism
history.text: At the council of Vaishali in c. 380 BC disputes over monastic rules began the split between the Sthavira elders and the Mahasanghika majority.

history.title: Ashoka's conversion
history.text: In c. 260 BC, after his bloody conquest of Kalinga, the Maurya emperor Ashoka embraced the Dharma, set up edicts across India and sent missions to Sri Lanka and Gandhara.

history.title: Indo-Greek Buddhism
history.text: In c. 150 BC the Indo-Greek king Menander, remembered as Milinda, debated the monk Nagasena, as Buddhism flourished in Bactria and Gandhara.

history.title: Kushans and the Silk Road
history.text: From c. 127 the Kushan emperor Kanishka patronised Buddhism; Gandhara art gave the Buddha a human image and monks carried the faith along the Silk Road to China.

history.title: Nalanda founded
history.text: In c. 427 the Gupta kings founded the monastery university of Nalanda in Bihar, which drew students from China, Korea and Tibet for 800 years.

history.title: Decline in India
history.text: In c. 1193 Turkic armies sacked Nalanda and Vikramashila; with Hindu revival and lost patronage, Buddhism nearly vanished from India outside the Himalayas.

history.title: Ambedkar's mass conversion
history.text: In 1956 B. R. Ambedkar and about 400,000 Dalits converted to Buddhism at Nagpur, reviving the faith in its homeland as a movement against caste.

denominations.name: Theravada Buddhism
denominations.text: The 'teaching of the elders', based on the Pali canon, followed in Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.

history.title: Mahinda reaches Sri Lanka
history.text: In c. 250 BC Ashoka's son Mahinda converted King Devanampiya Tissa at Anuradhapura, founding the Mahavihara monastery and Sri Lankan Buddhism.

history.title: Pali canon written down
history.text: In c. 29 BC monks at Aluvihare in Sri Lanka wrote down the Pali canon for the first time, the scripture of Theravada to this day.

history.title: Buddhaghosa's commentaries
history.text: In c. 430 the scholar Buddhaghosa wrote the Visuddhimagga and Pali commentaries at Anuradhapura, fixing Theravada doctrine.

history.title: Anawrahta of Pagan
history.text: In 1056 King Anawrahta of Pagan adopted Theravada under the monk Shin Arahan, making Burma a Theravada kingdom of thousands of temples.

history.title: Sri Lankan Sangha unified
history.text: In 1165 Parakramabahu I unified the Sri Lankan monastic orders under the Mahavihara, and its strict lineage became the model for Southeast Asia.

history.title: Sukhothai and the Thai
history.text: From c. 1279 King Ram Khamhaeng of Sukhothai patronised Sri Lankan-style Theravada, which became the religion of the Thai kingdoms.

history.title: Laos and Cambodia convert
history.text: In 1353 Fa Ngum founded Lan Xang in Laos with Theravada as its faith, and by then Cambodia too had turned from the Hindu and Mahayana cults of Angkor to Theravada.

history.title: Siam restores Lankan ordination
history.text: In 1753 Siamese monks led by Upali restored higher ordination in Kandy, founding the Siam Nikaya, Sri Lanka's largest monastic order.

history.title: Communist persecution
history.text: From 1975 the Khmer Rouge destroyed Cambodia's monasteries and killed most of its monks, and the new communist government of Laos restricted the Sangha.

history.title: Theravada today
history.text: Today about 150 million Theravada Buddhists form the majority in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, after Cambodia's revival in the 1980s and 1990s.

denominations.name: Mahayana Buddhism
denominations.text: The 'great vehicle' with its bodhisattvas and many sutras, including Chan or Zen and Pure Land, followed in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

history.title: Great Vehicle sutras
history.text: In c. AD 100 new sutras such as the Perfection of Wisdom and the Lotus Sutra spread in India, teaching the bodhisattva path; Nagarjuna soon gave Mahayana its philosophy.

history.title: Scriptures reach Luoyang
history.text: In 148 the Parthian monk An Shigao began translating Buddhist texts at Luoyang, and the Kushan monk Lokaksema soon followed with the first Mahayana sutras in Chinese.

history.title: Korea and Japan
history.text: Buddhism reached Korea in 372, and in 538 (or 552) the Korean kingdom of Baekje sent images and sutras to Japan, where Prince Shotoku promoted it from 594.

history.title: Tang golden age
history.text: In 629 Xuanzang set out for India to collect scriptures; under the Tang, Chinese schools such as Chan, Pure Land and Tiantai took shape.

history.title: Huichang persecution
history.text: In 845 Emperor Wuzong closed some 4,600 monasteries and defrocked over 260,000 monks and nuns; Chan and Pure Land survived best and came to dominate.

history.title: Ly dynasty in Vietnam
history.text: In 1009 the Ly dynasty, raised to power with the support of monks, made Mahayana Buddhism the court religion of Dai Viet.

history.title: Kamakura schools in Japan
history.text: From 1175 Honen founded Pure Land, followed by Eisai's and Dogen's Zen and Nichiren's Lotus school, bringing Buddhism to ordinary Japanese.

history.title: Joseon favours Confucianism
history.text: In 1392 Korea's new Joseon dynasty adopted Neo-Confucianism as state ideology and pushed Buddhist monasteries into the mountains.

history.title: Cultural Revolution
history.text: From 1966 the Cultural Revolution closed or destroyed temples across China, after communist rule began in 1949; Vietnam's communists restricted Buddhism from 1975.

history.title: Revival and reach today
history.text: Since the 1980s temples have reopened in China; Mahayana is the largest Buddhist tradition, with roughly 200 to 350 million followers in East Asia and Vietnam.

denominations.name: Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism
denominations.text: Tantric Buddhism led by lamas such as the Dalai Lama, followed in Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan and Buryatia.

history.title: Tantric Buddhism in India
history.text: In c. 700 tantric or Vajrayana Buddhism developed in India, using mantras, mandalas and guru initiation, and flourished under the Pala kings of Bengal.

history.title: Samye, first monastery
history.text: In c. 779 the Tibetan emperor Trisong Detsen founded Samye with Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava and made Buddhism the state religion of the Tibetan empire.

history.title: Tibetan empire collapses
history.text: In c. 842 the Tibetan empire broke apart after the murder of King Langdarma, remembered as a persecutor, and monastic Buddhism declined for over a century.

history.title: Atisha and second diffusion
history.text: In 1042 the Bengali master Atisha arrived in western Tibet; the revival gave rise to the Kadam, Sakya and Kagyu schools.

history.title: Phagpa and Kublai Khan
history.text: In 1260 Kublai Khan named the Sakya lama Phagpa his imperial preceptor, giving the Sakya rule over Tibet under the Yuan and Tibetan Buddhism a Mongol following.

history.title: Tsongkhapa's Gelug school
history.text: In 1409 the reformer Tsongkhapa founded Ganden monastery near Lhasa, beginning the Gelug or Yellow Hat school.

history.title: Dalai Lama title, Mongols convert
history.text: In 1578 the Mongol Altan Khan gave the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso the title Dalai Lama, and the Mongols converted to Tibetan Buddhism.

history.title: Dalai Lama rules Tibet
history.text: In 1642 the Fifth Dalai Lama became ruler of Tibet with Mongol help and began the Potala Palace, while in Bhutan the Zhabdrung had founded a Drukpa Kagyu state from 1616.

history.title: Exile to India
history.text: In 1959, after a failed uprising against Chinese rule, the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India; most Tibetan monasteries were destroyed in the Cultural Revolution.

history.title: Revival in Mongolia
history.text: Since 1990 monasteries have reopened in Mongolia, Buryatia, Kalmykia and Tuva; Vajrayana is also the state religion of Bhutan and lives on in Ladakh and the exile community.

denominations.name: Confucianism, Taoism and Chinese folk religion
denominations.text: China's blend of ancestor worship, Confucian ethics and Taoist practice, practised alongside Buddhism.

history.title: Confucius teaches
history.text: Confucius (551 to 479 BC) taught ritual, filial piety and virtuous rule in the state of Lu, building on Shang ancestor worship and the Zhou Mandate of Heaven.

history.title: Daodejing and Zhuangzi
history.text: In c. 350 BC the Daodejing attributed to Laozi and the writings of Zhuangzi took shape, the classic texts of Taoism and its ideal of harmony with the Dao.

history.title: Han state Confucianism
history.text: In 136 BC Emperor Wu of Han established official scholars of the Five Classics, making Confucianism the ideology of the Chinese state for two millennia.

history.title: Celestial Masters
history.text: In 142 Zhang Daoling claimed a revelation from the deified Laozi in Sichuan, founding the Way of the Celestial Masters, the first organised Taoist church.

history.title: Tang Three Teachings
history.text: The Tang dynasty from 618 honoured Laozi as ancestor of the imperial house, while Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism coexisted as the Three Teachings.

history.title: Neo-Confucian orthodoxy
history.text: In 1313 the Yuan made Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian commentaries the standard for the civil service exams, an orthodoxy that ruled Chinese learning until 1905.

history.title: Joseon Korea and Vietnam
history.text: From 1392 Joseon Korea, and later the Le dynasty of Vietnam from 1428, adopted Neo-Confucianism as state ideology, spreading ancestor rites across East Asia.

history.title: Exams abolished
history.text: In 1905 the Qing abolished the Confucian civil service exams, and the 1911 revolution ended the imperial rites to Heaven.

history.title: Cultural Revolution
history.text: From 1966 the Cultural Revolution attacked Confucius, temples and ancestral shrines, deepening the suppression of religion begun under communist rule in 1949.

history.title: Revival today
history.text: Since c. 1980 temples and ancestor rites have revived in China, and Chinese folk religion, Taoism and Confucian values remain strong in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore and the diaspora.

denominations.name: Shinto
denominations.text: Japan's worship of the kami at shrines, intertwined with Buddhism for a thousand years and made a state cult from 1868 to 1945.

history.title: Kami worship of Yamato
history.text: In c. 300 the Yamato rulers, buried in great kofun mounds, worshipped the kami of mountains, rivers and ancestors and traced their line to the sun goddess Amaterasu.

history.title: Buddhism joins the kami
history.text: In 587 the pro-Buddhist Soga clan defeated the Mononobe, and kami worship began a thousand-year blending with Buddhism.

history.title: Kojiki records the myths
history.text: In 712 the Kojiki and in 720 the Nihon Shoki recorded the kami myths and the imperial descent from Amaterasu; the Ise Grand Shrine had been rebuilt every 20 years since 690.

history.title: Engishiki shrine register
history.text: In 927 the Engishiki listed 2,861 shrines receiving state offerings, as kami came to be seen as local forms of Buddhas and bodhisattvas.

history.title: Meiji State Shinto
history.text: In 1868 the Meiji government separated Shinto from Buddhism and built State Shinto around worship of the emperor.

history.title: Shrines across the empire
history.text: After taking Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910, Japan built state shrines in its colonies, and in the 1930s pressed colonial subjects to attend them.

history.title: Shinto Directive
history.text: In December 1945 the US occupation abolished State Shinto, and in 1946 the emperor renounced divinity; shrines became private religious bodies.

history.title: Ise rebuilt again
history.text: In 2013 the Ise Grand Shrine was rebuilt for the 62nd time; most Japanese still visit some 80,000 shrines for festivals and New Year while calling themselves non-religious.

denominations.name: Christianity (before the Great Schism)
denominations.text: The one imperial church of the Roman world, before Catholics and Orthodox split in 1054.

history.title: Crucifixion of Jesus, c. 30
history.text: Jesus of Nazareth was crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30, and his followers began preaching his resurrection among the Jews of Judea and Galilee.

history.title: Paul's missions to the Gentiles
history.text: Around AD 50 Paul and other apostles carried the faith through Syria, Anatolia and Greece to Rome, founding mixed Jewish and Gentile churches in the cities of the empire.

history.title: Edict of Milan
history.text: Constantine and Licinius granted Christians legal freedom in 313, ending the persecutions and starting imperial patronage that let the church grow fast across the Roman world.

history.title: Council of Nicaea
history.text: The first ecumenical council, called by Constantine, condemned Arius and defined the Son as of one substance with the Father, setting the creed of mainstream Christianity.

history.title: State religion of Rome
history.text: Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire with the Edict of Thessalonica, and pagan sacrifices were banned in the following years.

history.title: Council of Chalcedon
history.text: Chalcedon defined Christ as one person in two natures; Egypt, Armenia and much of Syria rejected it, splitting off the Oriental Orthodox churches.

history.title: Baptism of Clovis, c. 496
history.text: Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptised a Nicene Christian in Reims, making Gaul a Catholic kingdom while most other Germanic rulers were still Arian.

history.title: Arab conquests begin
history.text: From the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 the Arab armies took Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa, and by 711 Spain, cutting the Christian world back to Europe and Anatolia.

history.title: Baptism of Kievan Rus, c. 988
history.text: After the conversion of Bulgaria (864) and the mission of Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs, Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev was baptised, bringing the Rus into Byzantine Christianity.

history.title: The Great Schism
history.text: Papal legates and Patriarch Michael Cerularius excommunicated each other in Constantinople, and the church split into a Latin Catholic West and a Greek Orthodox East.

denominations.name: Arian Christianity
denominations.text: Christians who held that the Son was created by the Father; condemned at Nicaea in 325 but the faith of the Goths, Vandals and Lombards until about 700.

history.title: Arius preaches in Alexandria, c. 318
history.text: The Alexandrian priest Arius taught that the Son was created by the Father and was not eternal, and his bishop Alexander condemned him, starting a controversy across the East.

history.title: Condemned at Nicaea
history.text: The Council of Nicaea rejected Arius's teaching and exiled him, but many eastern bishops and later the emperors Constantius II and Valens favoured Arian or compromise creeds.

history.title: Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths
history.text: Ulfilas, consecrated around 341, preached to the Goths north of the Danube and translated the Bible into Gothic, making the Goths and then other Germanic peoples Arian.

history.title: Defeat at Constantinople
history.text: Theodosius I and the Council of Constantinople reaffirmed the Nicene creed, and Arianism was outlawed in the empire, surviving mainly among the Germanic peoples on and beyond its borders.

history.title: Vandal kingdom in Africa
history.text: The Vandals under Gaiseric crossed from Spain in 429 and took Carthage in 439, ruling Roman Africa as Arians who often persecuted the Nicene clergy.

history.title: Ostrogothic Italy
history.text: Theodoric the Great, an Arian Ostrogoth, made himself king of Italy in 493, while Visigoths in Spain and Burgundians in Gaul also ruled as Arians over Nicene subjects.

history.title: Vandals and Ostrogoths destroyed
history.text: Justinian's general Belisarius ended the Vandal kingdom in 534, and the Ostrogoths were crushed by 553, returning Africa and Italy to the Nicene church.

history.title: Lombards invade Italy
history.text: The largely Arian Lombards under Alboin conquered much of northern and central Italy from 568, giving Arianism its last great kingdom.

history.title: Reccared's conversion
history.text: King Reccared led the Visigoths of Spain to Nicene Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo in 589, ending Arianism in the Iberian Peninsula.

history.title: End of Arianism, c. 680
history.text: Under Queen Theodelinda and later kings such as Aripert I the Lombards gradually became Catholic, and by the late 7th century Arianism had disappeared as an organised church.

denominations.name: Oriental Orthodoxy (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac)
denominations.text: The ancient churches that rejected the Council of Chalcedon in 451: the Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian and Syriac Orthodox churches.

history.title: Rejection of Chalcedon
history.text: Miaphysite Christians in Egypt and Syria refused Chalcedon's two natures formula, and the Coptic church of Alexandria, with its daughter church in Ethiopia, broke with Rome and Constantinople.

history.title: Armenia rejects Chalcedon
history.text: The Armenian church formally rejected Chalcedon at the First Council of Dvin around 506, keeping Armenia separate from the imperial church ever after.

history.title: Jacob Baradaeus and Nubia, c. 543
history.text: Jacob Baradaeus began ordaining a separate Syriac Orthodox hierarchy, and missions backed by Empress Theodora converted the Nubian kingdoms on the upper Nile.

history.title: Arab conquest of Egypt
history.text: The Arabs took Egypt in 641 and Syria shortly before; Copts and Syriacs kept their churches under Muslim rule but slowly became minorities over the following centuries.

history.title: Solomonic Ethiopia
history.text: The Solomonic dynasty took power in Ethiopia in 1270 and made the highland kingdom the great stronghold of Oriental Orthodoxy, with a revival of monasteries and church literature.

history.title: Nubian Christianity fades, c. 1500
history.text: After Makuria fell to Muslim rulers in the 14th century and Alodia collapsed around 1504, Christianity disappeared from Nubia, now Sudan.

history.title: Armenian and Syriac genocide
history.text: The Ottoman government killed about one million Armenians and many Syriac Christians from 1915, emptying eastern Anatolia of its ancient churches.

history.title: Ethiopian church independent
history.text: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received its own patriarch from the Coptic church in 1959, and the Eritrean church followed in 1993.

history.title: Today
history.text: Armenia regained independence in 1991 with its national church; today Oriental Orthodox Christians number roughly 60 million, most of them in Ethiopia, with large Coptic and Armenian communities.

denominations.name: Church of the East (Nestorian)
denominations.text: The Persian church whose missionaries reached India, Central Asia and Tang China.

history.title: Nestorius condemned at Ephesus
history.text: The Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorius of Constantinople, and his followers found refuge in the church of the Persian Empire, already organised at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410.

history.title: School moves to Nisibis
history.text: Emperor Zeno closed the School of Edessa in 489 and its teachers moved to Nisibis in Persia, as the Persian church adopted the dyophysite teaching associated with Nestorius.

history.title: Alopen reaches Tang China
history.text: The monk Alopen brought the faith to the Tang capital Chang'an in 635, as recorded on the Xi'an Stele of 781, while other missions served India and Central Asia.

history.title: Timothy I in Baghdad
history.text: Under the Abbasid caliphs the patriarchs moved to Baghdad, and Patriarch Timothy I (780 to 823) sent bishops to Central Asia, Tibet and China at the church's greatest reach.

history.title: Persecution in China
history.text: Emperor Wuzong's suppression of foreign religions in 845 effectively ended the church in China for centuries.

history.title: Conversion of the Keraits, c. 1007
history.text: The Kerait tribe of Mongolia converted around 1007, and the Naimans and Ongut followed, so many Mongol and Turkic nobles were Church of the East Christians in the 13th century.

history.title: Mongols turn to Islam
history.text: The Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295, followed by persecutions and then Timur's campaigns around 1400, which destroyed the church in Iran and Central Asia.

history.title: Schism and Chaldean Church
history.text: In 1552 part of the church chose Yohannan Sulaqa as patriarch and entered union with Rome, founding the Chaldean Catholic Church, while in India the Portuguese latinised the St Thomas Christians.

history.title: Assyrian genocide
history.text: During the First World War Ottoman and Kurdish forces killed many Assyrians in Hakkari and northwest Iran, and survivors fled to Iraq and later the West.

history.title: Today
history.text: The Assyrian Church of the East moved its patriarch back from Chicago to Erbil in 2015 and has a few hundred thousand members in Iraq, Iran, Syria, India and the diaspora.

denominations.name: Roman Catholicism
denominations.text: The Latin church led by the Pope in Rome, after the 1054 split with the Orthodox East.

history.title: The Great Schism
history.text: Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other in 1054, and the Latin church under the pope became a separate communion covering western and central Europe.

history.title: The Crusades
history.text: Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade at Clermont, and Latin crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 and set up Catholic states in the Levant that lasted until 1291.

history.title: Sack of Constantinople
history.text: The Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople and set up a Latin Empire there until 1261, deepening the rift with the Orthodox East.

history.title: Lithuania converts
history.text: Grand Duke Jogaila was baptised when he married Queen Jadwiga of Poland, making Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe, a Catholic land.

history.title: Granada and the New World
history.text: Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada, completing the Reconquista of Spain, and Columbus's voyage that year opened the Americas to Catholic conquest and missions.

history.title: The Reformation
history.text: Martin Luther's protest began the Reformation, and within decades the Catholic church lost northern Germany, Scandinavia, England, Scotland and the Netherlands.

history.title: Conquest of Mexico
history.text: Cortes took the Aztec capital in 1521 and Pizarro conquered the Inca from 1532, and friars made Spanish and Portuguese America the largest Catholic region of the world.

history.title: Council of Trent
history.text: The Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) reformed the church and defined doctrine against Protestantism, while the Jesuits led missions to Asia and won back Poland and much of central Europe.

history.title: Second Vatican Council
history.text: Vatican II (1962 to 1965) allowed the mass in local languages and opened dialogue with other churches, as the church grew rapidly in Africa and Asia.

history.title: Today
history.text: Leo XIV, born in the United States, was elected pope in 2025, leading about 1.4 billion Catholics, more than 40 percent of them in Latin America.

denominations.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
denominations.text: The Greek, Slavic and Romanian churches in communion with Constantinople, after the 1054 split with Rome.

history.title: The Great Schism
history.text: Patriarch Michael Cerularius and the papal legates excommunicated each other, and the Greek, Bulgarian and Rus churches in communion with Constantinople became the Orthodox East.

history.title: Crusaders take Constantinople
history.text: The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and imposed a Latin patriarch until 1261, leaving lasting bitterness against the Catholic West.

history.title: Serbian church autocephalous
history.text: Saint Sava became the first archbishop of an independent Serbian church in 1219, as Orthodoxy took deep national roots in the Balkans and among the Rus.

history.title: Fall of Constantinople
history.text: The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, and the Orthodox of the Balkans and Anatolia lived for centuries as a protected community under Muslim rule.

history.title: Moscow patriarchate
history.text: Moscow, now seeing itself as the Third Rome, gained its own patriarch in 1589, and Russian expansion carried Orthodoxy across Siberia to the Pacific and Alaska.

history.title: Balkan independence
history.text: The Greek war of independence from 1821, followed by Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria, created Orthodox nation states each with its own national church.

history.title: Bolshevik revolution
history.text: Soviet rule closed most churches and killed or imprisoned thousands of clergy, and after 1945 communist governments restricted Orthodoxy across eastern Europe.

history.title: Revival after communism
history.text: The fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 brought a large revival of church life in Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Georgia and the Balkans.

history.title: Today
history.text: Constantinople recognised an independent Orthodox Church of Ukraine in 2019, causing a break with Moscow; Orthodox Christians number about 220 to 260 million, most in eastern Europe.

denominations.name: Hussite (Utraquist) Christianity
denominations.text: The Bohemian reform church of Jan Hus's followers, a century before Luther, which gave the laity the communion cup.

history.title: Jan Hus preaches in Prague
history.text: The Prague priest Jan Hus took up John Wycliffe's ideas, attacking indulgences and the wealth of the clergy from the Bethlehem Chapel.

history.title: Hus burned at Constance
history.text: The Council of Constance condemned Hus and burned him as a heretic, turning Bohemian anger into a national religious movement.

history.title: Defenestration and revolution
history.text: Hussites threw Prague councillors from a window and took over Bohemia; their sign was the chalice, communion in both kinds for all.

history.title: Zizka defeats the crusades
history.text: Under Jan Zizka and Prokop the Great, Hussite armies with war wagons beat five papal crusades between 1420 and 1431.

history.title: Compacts of Basel
history.text: After the moderate Utraquists crushed the radical Taborites at Lipany in 1434, the Church accepted their chalice in the Compacts of Basel.

history.title: Peace of Kutna Hora
history.text: Bohemia's Catholic and Utraquist estates agreed to tolerate each other, a rare religious peace in medieval Europe.

history.title: Bohemian Confession
history.text: Utraquists, Lutherans and the Unity of Brethren joined in a common Protestant confession, confirmed by Rudolf II's Letter of Majesty in 1609.

history.title: White Mountain and suppression
history.text: The Protestant estates' defeat at White Mountain ended the Hussite church; the Habsburgs forced re-Catholicisation and exiled its leaders.

history.title: Remembered in Czechoslovakia
history.text: Hus became a national hero of independent Czechoslovakia, and the new Czechoslovak Hussite Church was founded in 1920.

denominations.name: Lutheranism
denominations.text: The first Protestant church, from Martin Luther's break with Rome, dominant in northern Germany and Scandinavia.

history.title: Ninety-five Theses
history.text: Martin Luther, a monk and professor in Wittenberg in Saxony, attacked the sale of indulgences, and his teaching of salvation by faith alone spread rapidly through print.

history.title: Diet of Worms
history.text: Luther refused to recant before Emperor Charles V and was outlawed, but protected by Frederick the Wise he translated the Bible into German.

history.title: Sweden breaks with Rome
history.text: Gustav Vasa began the Swedish Reformation at the Diet of Vasteras in 1527, bringing Sweden and Finland into the Lutheran fold, while Livonian towns also turned Lutheran.

history.title: Augsburg Confession
history.text: Philip Melanchthon presented the Augsburg Confession to the emperor, the defining statement of Lutheran faith, and many German princes and cities adopted it.

history.title: Denmark and Norway
history.text: Christian III made Lutheranism the state religion of Denmark, Norway and Iceland, so all of Scandinavia became Lutheran.

history.title: Peace of Augsburg
history.text: The Peace of Augsburg let each German prince choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his land, legally dividing the Holy Roman Empire.

history.title: Peace of Westphalia
history.text: The Thirty Years' War, in which Sweden's Gustavus Adolphus defended the Lutheran cause, ended in 1648 with the confessional map of Germany and the Baltic largely fixed.

history.title: Prussian Union
history.text: King Frederick William III merged Lutheran and Reformed churches in Prussia, prompting some Old Lutherans to emigrate.

history.title: Emigration to America, c. 1850
history.text: German and Scandinavian emigrants brought Lutheran churches to the American Midwest, while missions later built large churches in Ethiopia, Tanzania, Namibia and Indonesia.

history.title: Today
history.text: Sweden separated church and state in 2000; Lutherans number about 75 million, with old majorities in the Nordic countries and fast growth in Africa.

denominations.name: Anglicanism
denominations.text: The Church of England, separated from Rome by Henry VIII in 1534, and its daughter churches across the British Empire.

history.title: Act of Supremacy
history.text: Henry VIII broke with the pope over his divorce and Parliament made the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, followed by the dissolution of the monasteries.

history.title: Book of Common Prayer
history.text: Under Edward VI Archbishop Thomas Cranmer issued the Book of Common Prayer in English, giving the church a Protestant liturgy.

history.title: Catholic restoration under Mary
history.text: Mary I returned England to Rome and burned nearly 300 Protestants, including Cranmer, until her death in 1558.

history.title: Elizabethan Settlement
history.text: Elizabeth I restored the Church of England as a Protestant church with bishops, which also became the established, though minority, Church of Ireland.

history.title: Virginia colony
history.text: The Jamestown settlers brought the Church of England to America, where it became established in Virginia and other southern colonies.

history.title: Episcopal Church in America
history.text: After American independence the Protestant Episcopal Church was organised in 1789, the first Anglican church outside the British Isles independent of the crown.

history.title: First Lambeth Conference
history.text: Bishops from across the British Empire met at Lambeth Palace, forming what became the Anglican Communion of national churches.

history.title: Missions in Africa, c. 1900
history.text: Missionary societies built large Anglican churches in Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya under British colonial rule, which today hold most of the Communion's members.

history.title: Today
history.text: Disputes over sexuality led conservative churches, mostly African, to found GAFCON in 2008; the Communion has about 85 million members, the largest church being in Nigeria.

denominations.name: Reformed (Calvinist and Presbyterian)
denominations.text: John Calvin's Protestantism: the Swiss, Dutch, Scottish Presbyterian and Huguenot churches.

history.title: Calvin in Geneva
history.text: John Calvin published the Institutes of the Christian Religion and began his work in Geneva, building on Zwingli's reformation in Zurich from 1519.

history.title: Scottish Reformation
history.text: Led by John Knox, the Scottish Parliament abolished papal authority in 1560 and created a Presbyterian Church of Scotland.

history.title: French Wars of Religion
history.text: War broke out between Catholics and Calvinist Huguenots in France, ending with the Edict of Nantes in 1598, which granted the Huguenots limited toleration.

history.title: Dutch Republic
history.text: The northern Netherlands declared independence from Catholic Spain in 1581, and the Dutch Reformed Church became the public church of the republic.

history.title: Synod of Dort
history.text: The Synod of Dort (1618 to 1619) condemned the Arminians and defined strict Calvinist doctrine for the Reformed churches.

history.title: Puritan New England
history.text: English Puritans founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1630, while Scottish Presbyterians settled Ulster in the same decades.

history.title: Dutch Cape Colony
history.text: The Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town, and the Dutch Reformed Church became the church of the Afrikaners in South Africa.

history.title: Huguenot exodus
history.text: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, and about 200,000 Huguenots fled France to the Netherlands, Prussia, England and South Africa.

history.title: Presbyterian Korea
history.text: American Presbyterian missionaries arrived in Korea from 1884, and Presbyterianism became the largest Protestant church in South Korea.

history.title: Today
history.text: Reformed and Presbyterian churches number tens of millions, strong in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Scotland, South Korea, southern Africa and the United States.

denominations.name: Evangelical Protestantism
denominations.text: Later Protestant movements such as Baptists, Methodists and Pentecostals, strongest in the United States, Africa and Latin America today.

history.title: First Baptist church
history.text: English Separatists led by John Smyth in Amsterdam founded the first Baptist church, baptising only believing adults.

history.title: Baptists in America
history.text: Roger Williams founded the first Baptist church in America in Providence, Rhode Island, a colony built on religious freedom.

history.title: Wesley and Methodism
history.text: John Wesley's conversion in London began the Methodist revival, which with George Whitefield's preaching fed the Great Awakening in Britain and America.

history.title: Methodist Episcopal Church
history.text: American Methodists formed their own church in Baltimore in 1784, which grew to be the largest denomination in the United States by the mid 19th century.

history.title: Modern missions
history.text: William Carey founded the Baptist Missionary Society and sailed to India, starting a wave of evangelical missions to Asia, Africa and the Pacific.

history.title: Second Great Awakening
history.text: The Cane Ridge revival in Kentucky helped spread Baptists and Methodists across the American frontier, making evangelicalism the dominant faith of the United States.

history.title: Azusa Street revival
history.text: The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles launched Pentecostalism, which reached Brazil in 1911 with the Assemblies of God and soon spread worldwide.

history.title: Latin American boom, c. 1970
history.text: Pentecostal and evangelical churches grew rapidly in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa, winning large shares of Brazil, Guatemala, Nigeria and Kenya.

history.title: Today
history.text: Evangelical and Pentecostal Christians number several hundred million, most of them now in the Global South rather than Europe or North America.

denominations.name: Sunni Islam
denominations.text: The majority branch of Islam, which accepted the elected caliphs as Muhammad's successors.

history.title: The first caliphs
history.text: After Muhammad's death in 632 Abu Bakr was chosen as caliph and united Arabia; most Muslims accepted him and his successors, the root of Sunni Islam.

history.title: Arab conquests
history.text: Under Umar and Uthman the Arabs took Syria, Iraq and Egypt, and by 651 the Persian Empire, spreading Islam across the Middle East.

history.title: Umayyads reach Spain and Sindh
history.text: The Umayyad caliphate of Damascus crossed into Spain and conquered Sindh in 711, creating an empire from the Atlantic to Central Asia.

history.title: Abbasid caliphate
history.text: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and built Baghdad, where the Sunni schools of law and the hadith collections took shape.

history.title: Seljuks win at Manzikert
history.text: The Seljuk Turks defeated Byzantium at Manzikert in 1071, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement, after restoring Sunni rule in Baghdad over the Shia Buyids.

history.title: Delhi Sultanate
history.text: Turkic rulers founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206, bringing much of northern India under Sunni rule, later continued by the Mughals.

history.title: Mongols sack Baghdad
history.text: The Mongols destroyed Baghdad and ended the Abbasid caliphate, but the Golden Horde and the Ilkhans later converted, carrying Islam across the steppe.

history.title: Islam in Southeast Asia, c. 1400
history.text: Merchants and Sufis spread Islam through the trading ports of Southeast Asia, and Malacca's ruler converted, making the Malay world and later Java Muslim.

history.title: Ottomans take Constantinople
history.text: The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and in 1517 Egypt, leading the Sunni world as caliphs, while Spain fell to Christians in 1492 and Iran turned Shia in 1501.

history.title: End of the caliphate
history.text: Turkey abolished the Ottoman caliphate in 1924; today Sunnis are about 85 to 90 percent of nearly two billion Muslims, with Indonesia the largest Muslim country.

denominations.name: Twelver Shia Islam
denominations.text: The branch that follows Ali and twelve imams as Muhammad's rightful successors, state religion of Iran since 1501.

history.title: Karbala
history.text: Husayn, grandson of Muhammad and son of Ali, was killed by Umayyad troops at Karbala in Iraq, and mourning his death became the heart of Shia identity.

history.title: Occultation of the twelfth imam
history.text: The twelfth imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into hiding in 874 according to Twelver belief, and scholars came to lead the community in his absence.

history.title: Buyids in Baghdad
history.text: The Shia Buyid dynasty from Iran took control of Baghdad in 945 and ruled Iraq and western Iran until 1055, fostering Twelver scholarship.

history.title: Ilkhan Oljeitu converts
history.text: The Mongol Ilkhan Oljeitu adopted Twelver Shia Islam around 1310, an early royal conversion, though Iran remained mostly Sunni.

history.title: Safavid Iran
history.text: Shah Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty in 1501 and imposed Twelver Shia Islam on Iran and Azerbaijan, which became overwhelmingly Shia over the next two centuries.

history.title: Southern Iraq converts, c. 1800
history.text: Arab tribes of southern Iraq converted in large numbers in the 18th and 19th centuries, making Shia Muslims the majority in Iraq.

history.title: Iranian Revolution
history.text: Ayatollah Khomeini overthrew the shah and founded an Islamic Republic ruled by Shia clerics, backing Shia movements such as Hezbollah in Lebanon.

history.title: Today
history.text: After 2003 Shia parties came to power in Iraq; Twelvers are about 10 to 13 percent of Muslims, the majority in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Bahrain.

denominations.name: Ismaili Shia Islam
denominations.text: The Sevener branch of Shia Islam, faith of the Fatimid caliphs who ruled Egypt and North Africa from 909 to 1171.

history.title: Split over the imamate
history.text: When the imam Ja'far al-Sadiq died in 765, those who followed his son Ismail and grandson Muhammad broke with the Twelvers and became the Ismailis.

history.title: Fatimid caliphate founded
history.text: The Ismaili mission among the Kutama Berbers brought Abdallah al-Mahdi to power in Ifriqiya in 909, founding the Fatimid caliphate, while the Qarmatians held Bahrain.

history.title: Fatimids conquer Egypt
history.text: The Fatimids took Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo and al-Azhar, ruling also Syria, the Hejaz and Sicily at their height.

history.title: Hasan-i Sabbah at Alamut
history.text: Hasan-i Sabbah seized the fortress of Alamut in northern Iran in 1090, the base of the Nizari Ismaili state of castles in Iran and Syria.

history.title: Nizari and Musta'li split
history.text: A succession dispute in Cairo split the Ismailis into Nizaris, led from Alamut, and Musta'lis, whose Tayyibi branch survives as the Bohras of Yemen and India.

history.title: End of the Fatimids
history.text: Saladin abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and restored Sunni Islam in Egypt.

history.title: Mongols take Alamut
history.text: Hulagu's Mongols destroyed Alamut and the Nizari castles in Iran in 1256, and the Nizaris survived as scattered communities in Iran, Central Asia and India.

history.title: The Aga Khans
history.text: The Qajar shah granted the Nizari imam the title Aga Khan in 1817; Aga Khan I moved to India in the 1840s and built up communities in South Asia and East Africa.

history.title: Today
history.text: Aga Khan V succeeded his father in 2025 as imam of about 12 to 15 million Nizaris, living mainly in Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Tajikistan and the diaspora.

denominations.name: Ibadi Islam
denominations.text: A small early branch of Islam, distinct from both Sunni and Shia, majority in Oman.

history.title: Ibadis in Basra, c. 700
history.text: Moderate Kharijites led by scholars such as Jabir ibn Zayd in Basra, and named after Abdallah ibn Ibad, rejected both Umayyad rule and Kharijite violence.

history.title: First imamate in Oman
history.text: Oman's tribes elected al-Julanda ibn Mas'ud as Ibadi imam around 750, the start of a long tradition of elected imams in Oman.

history.title: Rustamid imamate
history.text: Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam founded an Ibadi imamate at Tahert in Algeria, ruling much of the central Maghreb, with Ibadis also strong in Jebel Nafusa in Libya.

history.title: Fatimids destroy Tahert
history.text: The Fatimids ended the Rustamid state in 909, and North African Ibadis withdrew to oases and islands such as the Mzab, Djerba and Jebel Nafusa.

history.title: Ya'ariba expel the Portuguese
history.text: The Ya'ariba imams, in power since 1624, took Muscat from the Portuguese in 1650 and then their East African ports, building an Omani maritime empire.

history.title: Al Said dynasty
history.text: Ahmad ibn Said founded the Al Said dynasty, which still rules Oman, after expelling the Persians.

history.title: Capital at Zanzibar
history.text: Sultan Said bin Sultan moved his court to Zanzibar around 1840, where an Omani Ibadi elite ruled the Swahili coast.

history.title: Zanzibar revolution
history.text: The Zanzibar revolution of 1964 overthrew the Arab sultan and ended Omani rule in East Africa.

history.title: Today
history.text: Sultan Qaboos, who took power in 1970, modernised Oman, the only country where Ibadis are the largest Muslim community, with small groups in Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Zanzibar.

denominations.name: Sikhism
denominations.text: Guru Nanak's monotheist faith of the Punjab, whose Sikh Empire ruled the region from 1799 to 1849.

history.title: Guru Nanak's revelation
history.text: In c. 1499 Guru Nanak had a revelation at Sultanpur Lodhi in the Punjab and began preaching one God beyond Hindu and Muslim divisions.

history.title: Adi Granth at Harmandir
history.text: In 1604 the fifth Guru, Arjan, installed the Adi Granth scripture in the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar; his execution under Jahangir in 1606 hardened Sikh resistance.

history.title: Khalsa founded
history.text: At Vaisakhi in 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Anandpur, a baptised brotherhood marked by the five Ks.

history.title: Scripture as eternal Guru
history.text: In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh died after naming the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as the eternal Guru; Banda Singh Bahadur then led a Sikh revolt in the Punjab.

history.title: Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire
history.text: In 1799 Ranjit Singh took Lahore and built a Sikh Empire across the Punjab to Kashmir and Peshawar, gilding the Harmandir into the Golden Temple.

history.title: British annexation
history.text: In 1849 Britain annexed the Punjab after two Anglo-Sikh wars; Sikhs became a pillar of the Indian Army and began emigrating across the empire.

history.title: Partition of Punjab
history.text: In 1947 Partition split the Punjab; nearly all Sikhs left the new Pakistan, concentrating the faith in Indian Punjab.

history.title: Operation Blue Star
history.text: In June 1984 the Indian army stormed the Golden Temple; Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was killed by her Sikh bodyguards, followed by anti-Sikh riots in Delhi.

history.title: Sikhs today
history.text: Today about 25 to 30 million Sikhs live worldwide, a majority in Indian Punjab, with large communities in Canada, Britain and the United States.

denominations.name: Secular or state atheism
denominations.text: Communist states that suppressed religion, and societies where most people now follow none.

history.title: Bolshevik revolution
history.text: Lenin's Bolsheviks separated church and state, seized church property and began a campaign against religion in Russia.

history.title: Soviet anti-religious campaign
history.text: The 1929 law on religious associations and the League of the Militant Godless led to mass closures of churches, mosques and synagogues and the killing of clergy in the 1930s.

history.title: Communist bloc expands
history.text: After 1945 communist regimes took over eastern Europe and in 1949 Mao founded the People's Republic of China, imposing state atheism on a large part of the world.

history.title: Cultural Revolution
history.text: Red Guards in China destroyed temples, churches and mosques from 1966, and religious practice was almost wholly banned until the late 1970s.

history.title: Albania bans religion
history.text: Enver Hoxha declared Albania the world's first atheist state in 1967 and closed every place of worship.

history.title: Indochina
history.text: Communist victories in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia in 1975 brought restrictions on Buddhism and Christianity, and the Khmer Rouge tried to wipe out religion.

history.title: Fall of Soviet Union
history.text: The collapse of communism in Europe brought religious revivals, though the Czech Republic, Estonia and eastern Germany stayed largely non-religious.

history.title: Today
history.text: Censuses show no religion rising in the West, with fewer than half of England and Wales Christian in 2021; about a quarter of the world is unaffiliated, most in China.

zones.name: New York City and New Jersey
Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro
New Britain, New Ireland and Bougainville
Central Switzerland (Lucerne and the Forest Cantons)

stories.name: Judaism
stories.summary: Judaism grew out of the worship of the God of Israel among the peoples of ancient Canaan. Exile, the loss of the Temple and centuries of dispersal turned it into a faith centred on scripture, law and community, carried by Jews across the Middle East, Europe and later the Americas.

steps.label: c. 1200 BC
steps.title: Israel in the hills of Canaan
steps.text: Villages of a people called Israel appear in the Canaanite highlands, and an Egyptian victory stele of c. 1208 BC names them for the first time. Their worship of Yahweh slowly set them apart from neighbouring Canaanite cults.

sites.name: Shiloh
sites.text: An early Israelite sanctuary which, according to the Bible, housed the Ark of the Covenant.

sites.name: Thebes
sites.text: Where the Merneptah Stele, the earliest known mention of Israel, was found.

steps.label: c. 960 BC
steps.title: Kingdoms and the First Temple
steps.text: According to the Bible, Solomon built the First Temple in Jerusalem, which became the centre of worship. The northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC, leaving Judah and Jerusalem as the heart of the faith.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.text: Capital of Judah and site of the First Temple.

sites.name: Samaria
sites.text: Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, taken by Assyria in 722 BC.

steps.label: 586 BC
steps.title: Exile in Babylon
steps.text: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and deported much of Judah's elite. In exile, priests and scribes gathered and shaped many of the texts of the Hebrew Bible, and after Persia's Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC many returned to rebuild the Temple.

sites.name: Babylon
sites.text: Centre of the exiled Judean community.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.text: The Second Temple was completed here around 516 BC.

steps.label: 167 BC
steps.title: Maccabees and the wider diaspora
steps.text: Under Greek rule, the Maccabean revolt won back Jewish control of the Temple, remembered in the festival of Hanukkah. Large Jewish communities now lived in Alexandria, Babylonia, Syria and Asia Minor, and the Bible was translated into Greek.

sites.name: Modiin
sites.text: Home of the Maccabee family, where the revolt began.

sites.name: Alexandria
sites.text: Its large Jewish community produced the Greek Septuagint.

steps.label: AD 70
steps.title: The Temple falls, the rabbis rebuild
steps.text: Rome destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70 and crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135. Without a Temple, rabbis organised Judaism around prayer, study and law, compiling the Mishnah around AD 200.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.text: The Second Temple was destroyed by Roman legions in AD 70.

sites.name: Yavne
sites.text: Seat of the rabbinic academy that reorganised Jewish life after 70.

sites.name: Rome
sites.text: The Arch of Titus shows Temple treasures carried in triumph.

steps.label: c. AD 500
steps.title: The Babylonian Talmud
steps.text: The great academies of Babylonia completed the Talmud, which became the core text of Jewish law and learning. Jewish communities stretched from Spain and North Africa to Persia and Yemen.

sites.name: Sura
sites.text: One of the two leading Babylonian academies.

sites.name: Pumbedita
sites.text: The other great academy, near modern Fallujah.

steps.label: c. 1000 to 1200
steps.title: Sephardim and Ashkenazim
steps.text: In Muslim Spain, Jewish poets and thinkers such as Maimonides flourished, while Ashkenazi communities grew in the Rhineland and northern France. The First Crusade of 1096 brought massacres of Rhineland Jews.

sites.name: Cordoba
sites.text: Birthplace of the philosopher and legal scholar Maimonides in 1138.

sites.name: Mainz
sites.text: With Speyer and Worms, a founding centre of Ashkenazi Jewry.

sites.name: Fustat (Old Cairo)
sites.text: The Cairo Geniza preserved a thousand years of Jewish documents.

steps.label: 1290 to 1500s
steps.title: Expulsions and new homes
steps.text: Jews were expelled from England in 1290, France in 1306 and 1394, Spain in 1492 and Portugal in 1497. Sephardic exiles found refuge in the Ottoman Empire and North Africa, while Ashkenazim moved east into Poland and Lithuania.

moves.label: Sephardic exile to the Ottoman Empire

sites.name: Granada
sites.text: The Alhambra Decree expelling Spain's Jews was signed here in 1492.

sites.name: Thessaloniki
sites.text: Became a largely Sephardic Jewish city under Ottoman rule.

sites.name: Safed
sites.text: A centre of Kabbalah mysticism in the 1500s.

steps.label: 1881 to 1924
steps.title: Mass migration and Zionism
