steps.text: Pogroms and poverty in the Russian Empire pushed over two million Jews to emigrate, mostly to the United States. In 1897 Theodor Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress, calling for a Jewish homeland.

sites.name: New York
sites.text: The Lower East Side became the largest Jewish community in the world.

sites.name: Basel
sites.text: Site of the First Zionist Congress in 1897.

steps.label: 1941 to today
steps.title: The Holocaust and the State of Israel
steps.text: Nazi Germany murdered about six million Jews in the Holocaust. The State of Israel was founded in 1948, and most Jews from Arab lands and Iran later moved there, so that Israel and the United States now hold most of the world's roughly 15 million Jews.

sites.name: Auschwitz
sites.text: The largest Nazi death camp, where about one million Jews were killed.

sites.name: Tel Aviv
sites.text: Israel's independence was declared here on 14 May 1948.

stories.name: Zoroastrianism
stories.summary: Zoroastrianism follows the teachings of the prophet Zarathustra, who preached worship of the wise lord Ahura Mazda and the struggle of truth against falsehood. It was the state faith of great Persian empires before Islam, and today survives in Iran and among the Parsis of India and their global diaspora.

steps.label: c. 1500 to 1000 BC
steps.title: Zarathustra's hymns
steps.text: The prophet Zarathustra composed the Gathas, hymns in an ancient Iranian language, somewhere in eastern Iran or Central Asia. Scholars debate his dates, but most place him in the late second millennium BC.

sites.name: Balkh (Bactria)
sites.text: Later tradition linked Zarathustra's mission to this region.

steps.label: c. 550 to 330 BC
steps.title: Faith of the Persian kings
steps.text: The Achaemenid kings of Persia, from Darius onward, credited their rule to Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions. Magi priests served the faith across an empire that stretched from Egypt to India.

sites.name: Persepolis
sites.text: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid kings.

sites.name: Behistun
sites.text: Darius's great inscription credits his victories to Ahura Mazda.

steps.label: 330 BC
steps.title: Alexander and the Parthians
steps.text: Alexander the Great burned Persepolis, and later tradition blamed him for the loss of sacred texts. The faith endured among Iranians under Greek and then Parthian rule.

sites.name: Persepolis
sites.text: Burned by Alexander's army in 330 BC.

steps.label: AD 224
steps.title: State church of the Sasanians
steps.text: The Sasanian dynasty made Zoroastrianism the official religion of Iran, with a powerful priesthood and great fire temples. The Avesta, long passed on orally, was eventually written down in a special script.

sites.name: Naqsh-e Rostam
sites.text: Royal reliefs and the inscription of the high priest Kartir.

sites.name: Adur Gushnasp
sites.text: One of the three great fire temples, at Takht-e Soleyman.

sites.name: Ctesiphon
sites.text: The Sasanian capital on the Tigris.

steps.label: AD 651
steps.title: The Arab conquest
steps.text: The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651 as Arab armies conquered Iran. Over the following centuries most Iranians converted to Islam, and Zoroastrians became a minority centred on Yazd and Kerman.

sites.name: Merv
sites.text: Where Yazdegerd III died in 651.

sites.name: Yazd
sites.text: A lasting heartland of Iran's Zoroastrian community.

steps.label: c. 8th to 10th century
steps.title: The Parsis sail to India
steps.text: According to the Qissa-i Sanjan, a group of Zoroastrians left Iran by sea and were granted refuge on the coast of Gujarat. Their descendants became known as the Parsis.

sites.name: Sanjan
sites.text: Traditional landing place of the first Parsi settlers.

sites.name: Udvada
sites.text: Home of the Iranshah, the most sacred Parsi fire, since 1742.

steps.label: 1800s
steps.title: The Parsis of Bombay
steps.text: Parsis prospered as merchants and industrialists in British Bombay, founding firms such as Tata. They also funded relief for the much poorer Zoroastrians of Qajar Iran.

sites.name: Mumbai
sites.text: Home to the largest Zoroastrian community in the world.

steps.label: 1979 to today
steps.title: A small global community
steps.text: After the Iranian Revolution many Zoroastrians emigrated, joining Parsis who had settled in Britain, North America and Australia. The worldwide community numbers perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 people.

sites.name: Yazd
sites.text: Its Atash Behram fire is said to have burned since the 5th century.

sites.name: London
sites.text: Home to one of the oldest Zoroastrian associations in the West, founded in 1861.

stories.name: Hinduism
stories.summary: Hinduism has no single founder; it grew from the Vedic religion of ancient north India and absorbed many local traditions. Its scriptures, temples and devotional movements shaped South and Southeast Asia, and today about 1.2 billion Hindus live mainly in India and Nepal, with a large global diaspora.

steps.label: c. 2600 to 1900 BC
steps.title: The Indus cities
steps.text: The Indus Valley Civilisation built planned cities with great baths and fire altars. Some scholars see roots of later Hindu practice here, but its script is undeciphered and its religion remains uncertain.

sites.name: Mohenjo-daro
sites.text: Its Great Bath may have been used for ritual purification.

sites.name: Harappa
sites.text: One of the largest Indus cities.

steps.label: c. 1500 to 1000 BC
steps.title: The Vedas
steps.text: Indo-Aryan speakers in the Punjab composed the hymns of the Rig Veda, centred on fire sacrifice and gods such as Agni and Indra. The hymns were passed on orally by Brahmin priests for many centuries.

sites.name: Sapta Sindhu (Punjab)
sites.text: The land of seven rivers praised in the Rig Veda.

steps.label: c. 800 to 300 BC
steps.title: Upanishads on the Ganges
steps.text: As kingdoms grew along the Ganges, the Upanishads explored ideas of karma, rebirth and liberation (moksha) and the unity of the self with ultimate reality (Brahman). The same age produced rival movements such as Buddhism and Jainism.

sites.name: Varanasi
sites.text: One of the oldest living cities and Hinduism's holiest place to die.

steps.label: c. AD 320 to 550
steps.title: The classical age
steps.text: Under the Gupta kings the Mahabharata, Ramayana and early Puranas took their lasting form. Worship of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess in stone temples became central.

sites.name: Deogarh
sites.text: Its Dashavatara temple is among the earliest surviving stone Hindu temples.

sites.name: Ujjain
sites.text: A sacred city and Gupta centre of learning.

steps.label: c. AD 100 to 1200
steps.title: Across the Bay of Bengal
steps.text: Traders and Brahmins carried Hindu ideas of kingship and worship to Southeast Asia. Funan, Champa, Java and the Khmer Empire built great temples, culminating in Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu in the 1100s.

sites.name: Angkor Wat
sites.text: Built by Suryavarman II and dedicated to Vishnu.

sites.name: Prambanan
sites.text: A great Shiva temple complex in Java, built in the 800s.

sites.name: My Son
sites.text: Temple sanctuary of the kings of Champa.

steps.label: c. 700 to 1200
steps.title: Devotion and great temples
steps.text: Tamil poet-saints spread bhakti, loving devotion to Shiva or Vishnu, and the philosopher Shankara taught non-dual Vedanta. The Chola kings raised vast temples such as the Brihadisvara at Thanjavur, completed in 1010.

sites.name: Thanjavur
sites.text: The Chola Brihadisvara temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

sites.name: Kalady
sites.text: Traditional birthplace of Adi Shankara.

steps.label: 1206 to 1700s
steps.title: Under sultans and Mughals
steps.text: Much of north India came under Muslim rulers, yet Hindus remained the great majority. Vijayanagara in the south was a major Hindu empire, and bhakti poets such as Kabir, Mirabai and Tulsidas reached ordinary people in their own languages. In Southeast Asia, Buddhism and Islam displaced Hinduism except on Bali.

sites.name: Hampi
sites.text: Capital of the Vijayanagara Empire until 1565.

sites.name: Vrindavan
sites.text: A centre of Krishna devotion revived in the 1500s.

steps.label: 1838 to 1917
steps.title: Indentured labour diaspora
steps.text: After slavery was abolished, Britain shipped over a million Indian indentured workers to plantations in the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius, East Africa and Natal. They carried their temples and festivals with them.

sites.name: Port of Spain
sites.text: Trinidad's Indian community is now about a third of the population.

sites.name: Durban
sites.text: Home to the largest Indian community in Africa.

steps.label: 1893 to today
steps.title: A world religion
steps.text: Vivekananda introduced Vedanta to the West at Chicago in 1893, and Gandhi drew on Hindu ideals in the independence struggle. Partition in 1947 uprooted millions, and today about 1.2 billion Hindus live mostly in India and Nepal, with growing communities in Britain and North America.

sites.name: Chicago
sites.text: Vivekananda's speech at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions.

sites.name: New Delhi
sites.text: Capital of independent India from 1947.

stories.name: Buddhism
stories.summary: Buddhism began with Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, who taught a path to freedom from suffering in northern India. Spread by monks, merchants and kings along the Silk Road and the sea lanes, it became a dominant faith across East and Southeast Asia, even as it faded in its Indian homeland.

steps.label: c. 5th century BC
steps.title: The Buddha's awakening
steps.text: Siddhartha Gautama, a prince of the Shakya clan, left home to seek an end to suffering and attained awakening at Bodh Gaya. He taught the Four Noble Truths and founded a community of monks and nuns.

sites.name: Lumbini
sites.text: Traditional birthplace of the Buddha.

sites.name: Bodh Gaya
sites.text: Where he attained awakening under the Bodhi tree.

sites.name: Sarnath
sites.text: Site of his first sermon.

steps.label: c. 260 BC
steps.title: Ashoka's dhamma
steps.text: Horrified by his conquest of Kalinga, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka embraced Buddhism and carved edicts across India. Tradition says his son Mahinda carried the teaching to Sri Lanka.

sites.name: Sanchi
sites.text: Its Great Stupa was begun under Ashoka.

sites.name: Pataliputra
sites.text: Ashoka's capital, modern Patna.

steps.label: c. AD 50 to 200
steps.title: Along the Silk Road
steps.text: Under the Kushan kings Gandhara became a centre of Buddhist art and of the new Mahayana movement. Monks and merchants carried the teaching across Central Asia into China.

sites.name: Taxila
sites.text: A great Gandharan monastic and trading city.

sites.name: Luoyang
sites.text: Home of the White Horse Temple, traditionally China's first Buddhist temple.

steps.label: AD 372 to 552
steps.title: China, Korea and Japan
steps.text: Buddhism flourished in China after the fall of the Han, and reached Korea in 372 and Japan in the 500s. Sea routes also carried it to Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka.

sites.name: Longmen Grottoes
sites.text: Thousands of Buddhist carvings begun in the late 400s.

sites.name: Asuka
sites.text: Early Japanese capital where Buddhism won court patronage.

steps.label: c. AD 630 to 850
steps.title: Pilgrims and Tibet
steps.text: The Chinese monk Xuanzang walked to India to study at Nalanda, the great Buddhist university. Tibet adopted Buddhism under its kings, and in Java the Sailendra dynasty built Borobudur around 800.

sites.name: Nalanda
sites.text: A monastic university that drew students from across Asia.

sites.name: Borobudur
sites.text: The world's largest Buddhist monument.

sites.name: Samye
sites.text: Tibet's first monastery, founded around 779.

steps.label: c. 1000 to 1300
steps.title: Decline in India, Theravada rises
steps.text: Buddhism faded in India as Hindu devotion revived, and Turkish raids destroyed Nalanda around 1193. Meanwhile Theravada Buddhism spread from Sri Lanka to Burma, Thailand and Cambodia, and Zen and Pure Land schools grew in Japan.

sites.name: Bagan
sites.text: Thousands of temples built by Burmese kings from the 1000s.

sites.name: Bayon, Angkor Thom
sites.text: Temple of the Buddhist Khmer king Jayavarman VII.

steps.title: The Dalai Lamas and the Mongols
steps.text: The Mongol ruler Altan Khan gave the title Dalai Lama to the Tibetan teacher Sonam Gyatso in 1578, and Tibetan Buddhism spread across Mongolia. In Korea, by contrast, the Joseon kings favoured Confucianism and restricted Buddhism.

sites.name: Lhasa
sites.text: The Potala Palace became the Dalai Lamas' seat in the 1600s.

sites.name: Erdene Zuu
sites.text: Mongolia's first great monastery, founded in 1585.

steps.label: 1950s to today
steps.title: Upheaval and a global audience
steps.text: Communist governments suppressed Buddhism in China, Mongolia and Cambodia, and the Dalai Lama fled into exile in 1959. In 1956 B. R. Ambedkar led hundreds of thousands of Dalits to convert in India, while meditation and Zen won followers in the West.

sites.name: Nagpur
sites.text: Ambedkar's mass conversion ceremony, 14 October 1956.

sites.name: Dharamsala
sites.text: Seat of the Dalai Lama in exile.

stories.name: Christianity
stories.summary: Christianity began with the followers of Jesus of Nazareth, who proclaimed him the Messiah after his crucifixion in Jerusalem. From a small Jewish movement it became the religion of the Roman Empire, then of Europe, and through missions and colonisation it became the world's largest faith, with about 2.4 billion adherents.

steps.label: c. AD 30
steps.title: Jesus of Nazareth
steps.text: Jesus, a Jewish teacher from Galilee, preached the coming kingdom of God and was crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate. His followers proclaimed that he had risen from the dead.

sites.name: Nazareth
sites.text: Jesus's hometown in Galilee.

sites.name: Capernaum
sites.text: Centre of his preaching by the Sea of Galilee.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.text: Where he was crucified, c. AD 30 to 33.

steps.label: c. AD 45 to 64
steps.title: Paul and the first churches
steps.text: Followers in Antioch were first called Christians, and the apostle Paul founded churches in Asia Minor and Greece and welcomed non-Jews. Tradition holds that Peter and Paul were martyred in Rome under Nero.

sites.name: Antioch
sites.text: Base of Paul's missions.

sites.name: Ephesus
sites.text: Paul lived and taught here for over two years.

sites.name: Rome
sites.text: Traditional site of the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul.

steps.label: c. AD 100 to 300
steps.title: Growth under persecution
steps.text: Despite periodic persecution, churches spread to Egypt, North Africa, Gaul, Spain and Mesopotamia. Armenia became the first kingdom to adopt Christianity, traditionally in 301.

sites.name: Carthage
sites.text: Home of Tertullian and Cyprian, leaders of Latin Christianity.

sites.name: Alexandria
sites.text: A great centre of Christian theology and of the Coptic church.

sites.name: Lyon
sites.text: Scene of the martyrs of 177 in Gaul.

steps.label: AD 313 to 380
steps.title: Religion of the empire
steps.text: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 and called the Council of Nicaea in 325. In 380 Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the state religion, and the kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia also converted.

sites.name: Constantinople
sites.text: Constantine's new Christian capital, dedicated in 330.

sites.name: Nicaea
sites.text: The first ecumenical council defined the Nicene Creed in 325.

sites.name: Aksum
sites.text: King Ezana adopted Christianity around 330.

steps.label: c. AD 400 to 900
steps.title: Europe converts, the East reaches China
steps.text: Missionaries such as Patrick, Augustine of Canterbury and Boniface converted the peoples of northern Europe, and Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800. Arab conquests made the Middle East and North Africa Muslim-ruled, while the Church of the East reached China.

moves.label: Church of the East to China

sites.name: Canterbury
sites.text: Augustine founded the English church here in 597.

sites.name: Rome
sites.text: Charlemagne was crowned emperor by the pope on Christmas Day 800.

sites.name: Xi'an
sites.text: A stele of 781 records the Church of the East in Tang China.

steps.label: AD 966 to 1054
steps.title: The north and east, then schism
steps.text: Poland, Kievan Rus', Hungary and Scandinavia adopted Christianity between the 960s and the 1000s. In 1054 the Latin church of Rome and the Greek church of Constantinople split into Catholic and Orthodox.

sites.name: Kyiv
sites.text: Prince Vladimir accepted baptism for his people in 988.

sites.name: Constantinople
sites.text: Mutual excommunications in 1054 marked the Great Schism.

steps.label: 1517 to 1600
steps.title: Reformation and the Americas
steps.text: Martin Luther's protest in 1517 launched the Protestant Reformation, which won much of northern Europe, while the Catholic Church renewed itself at Trent. Spanish and Portuguese missions carried Catholicism to the Americas, the Philippines and parts of Asia.

sites.name: Wittenberg
sites.text: Luther posted his 95 Theses here in 1517.

sites.name: Geneva
sites.text: John Calvin's base for Reformed Protestantism.

sites.name: Mexico City
sites.text: Centre of the Spanish missions, and of devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe.

steps.label: 1700s to 1800s
steps.title: Missions and settlers
steps.text: Revivals swept Britain and North America, and European settlers took their churches to North America, southern Africa and Australia. Protestant and Catholic missionaries worked across Africa, the Pacific and Asia, often alongside colonial expansion.

sites.name: Freetown
sites.text: Samuel Ajayi Crowther, later the first African Anglican bishop, was trained here.

sites.name: Tahiti
sites.text: London Missionary Society missionaries arrived in 1797.

steps.label: 1900s to today
steps.title: A global faith
steps.text: Pentecostalism spread worldwide from a 1906 revival in Los Angeles, and Communist states persecuted churches in Russia and Eastern Europe. By 2000 most Christians lived in Africa, Latin America and Asia rather than Europe.

sites.name: Los Angeles
sites.text: The Azusa Street Revival of 1906 helped launch Pentecostalism.

sites.name: Vatican City
sites.text: The Second Vatican Council (1962 to 1965) reshaped Catholic worship.

sites.name: Lagos
sites.text: Nigeria now has one of the largest Christian populations in the world.

stories.name: Islam
stories.summary: Islam began with the revelations received by the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca from 610. Within a century Arab conquests carried it from Spain to Central Asia, and traders, scholars and Sufi teachers later spread it across Africa and Asia; today about 1.9 billion Muslims make it the world's second-largest faith.

steps.label: AD 610
steps.title: The first revelation
steps.text: Muslims believe the angel Gabriel brought the first verses of the Quran to Muhammad in a cave near Mecca in 610. His preaching of one God won followers but also opposition, and around 615 some believers sought refuge in Christian Aksum.

sites.name: Mecca
sites.text: Muhammad's birthplace and home of the Kaaba.

sites.name: Cave of Hira
sites.text: Where the first revelation is said to have come.

steps.label: AD 622
steps.title: The Hijra to Medina
steps.text: Muhammad and his followers migrated to Medina in 622, the year from which the Islamic calendar is counted. He returned to Mecca in 630, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had joined the new community.

sites.name: Medina
sites.text: Site of the first Muslim community and of the Prophet's Mosque.

steps.label: AD 632 to 651
steps.title: The early conquests
steps.text: Under the first caliphs, Arab armies defeated both Byzantium and Persia, taking Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Iran within twenty years. Conversion of these lands' peoples took place gradually over the following centuries.

sites.name: Yarmouk
sites.text: Decisive Arab victory over Byzantium in 636.

sites.name: Fustat
sites.text: Founded in 641 as the Arab capital of Egypt.

steps.label: AD 656 to 680
steps.title: Karbala and the Sunni and Shia split
steps.text: Disputes over who should lead the community led to civil war, and Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, was murdered in 661. The killing of his son Husayn at Karbala in 680 became the defining moment for Shia Muslims, while the majority became known as Sunni.

sites.name: Karbala
sites.text: Where Husayn and his companions were killed in 680.

sites.name: Kufa
sites.text: Ali's capital and an early Shia centre.

sites.name: Damascus
sites.text: Capital of the Umayyad caliphs.

steps.label: AD 711 to 762
steps.title: From Spain to the Indus
steps.text: Umayyad armies crossed into Spain and reached Sindh in 711 and Transoxiana soon after. The Abbasids took power in 750 and built Baghdad, which became a centre of learning.

sites.name: Cordoba
sites.text: Capital of al-Andalus and its Great Mosque.

sites.name: Kairouan
sites.text: Founded around 670, the base for conquests in the Maghreb.

sites.name: Baghdad
sites.text: Founded in 762 as the Abbasid capital.

steps.label: 1000 to 1300
steps.title: Turks, sultans and caravans
steps.text: Turkish dynasties carried Islam into Anatolia after Manzikert in 1071 and into north India, where the Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1206. Trans-Saharan merchants brought Islam to West African courts, and the Shia Fatimids ruled Egypt from 969 to 1171.

sites.name: Manzikert
sites.text: Seljuk victory over Byzantium in 1071 opened Anatolia.

sites.name: Delhi
sites.text: The Qutb Minar marks the founding of Muslim rule in Delhi.

steps.label: 1300 to 1600
steps.title: Trade, empires and the Safavids
steps.text: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage of 1324 showed the wealth of Muslim Mali, and Indian Ocean merchants and Sufis spread Islam to the Swahili coast, Malacca and Java. The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, Granada fell to Spain in 1492, and from 1501 the Safavids made Shia Islam the faith of Iran.

sites.name: Timbuktu
sites.text: A centre of Islamic scholarship in Mali and Songhai.

sites.name: Malacca
sites.text: Its sultanate spread Islam through the Malay world.

sites.name: Isfahan
sites.text: Safavid capital and showpiece of Shia Iran.

steps.label: 1900s to today
steps.title: Nation states and migration
steps.text: The Ottoman caliphate was abolished in 1924, Pakistan was founded as a Muslim homeland in 1947, and Iran's 1979 revolution created an Islamic republic. Migration built large communities in Europe, and Indonesia is now the largest Muslim nation.

sites.name: Tehran
sites.text: Centre of the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

sites.name: Jakarta
sites.text: The Istiqlal Mosque serves the world's most populous Muslim nation.

stories.name: Sikhism
stories.summary: Sikhism was founded in the Punjab by Guru Nanak, who taught devotion to one God, honest work and the equality of all people. Shaped by ten Gurus and the scripture Guru Granth Sahib, it now has about 25 million followers, most in Indian Punjab and many in Britain, Canada and the United States.

steps.label: c. 1499
steps.title: Guru Nanak's call
steps.text: Guru Nanak, born in 1469 near Lahore, had a profound spiritual experience at Sultanpur Lodhi around 1499. He proclaimed that there is no Hindu and no Muslim, teaching that one God is found through devotion and service.

sites.name: Nankana Sahib
sites.text: Birthplace of Guru Nanak, now in Pakistan.

sites.name: Sultanpur Lodhi
sites.text: Where Nanak's mission began.

steps.label: c. 1500 to 1539
steps.title: Journeys and Kartarpur
steps.text: According to tradition Nanak made long journeys, as far as Mecca, Baghdad and the Himalaya, before settling at Kartarpur. There his followers farmed, sang hymns together and shared the communal kitchen, the langar.

sites.name: Kartarpur
sites.text: The community Nanak founded, where he died in 1539.

steps.title: The Adi Granth and the Golden Temple
steps.text: The fifth Guru, Arjan, completed the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar and compiled the hymns of the Gurus and other saints into the Adi Granth in 1604. He was executed under the Mughal emperor Jahangir in 1606.

sites.name: Amritsar
sites.text: The Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, Sikhism's holiest shrine.

sites.name: Lahore
sites.text: Where Guru Arjan died in Mughal custody in 1606.

steps.title: The Khalsa
steps.text: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, a community of initiated Sikhs who keep the five articles of faith, at Anandpur in 1699. Before his death in 1708 he declared the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib, to be the eternal Guru.

sites.name: Anandpur Sahib
sites.text: Birthplace of the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699.

sites.name: Nanded
sites.text: Where Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708.

steps.label: 1799 to 1849
steps.title: The Sikh Empire
steps.text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh took Lahore in 1799 and built a powerful kingdom across the Punjab. After two wars it was annexed by Britain in 1849.

sites.name: Lahore
sites.text: Capital of the Sikh Empire.

steps.label: c. 1870 to 1914
steps.title: Soldiers and settlers abroad
steps.text: Sikhs served in large numbers in the British Indian Army and emigrated to Malaya, East Africa, Canada and California. In 1914 the Komagata Maru, carrying mostly Sikh passengers, was turned away from Vancouver.

sites.name: Vancouver
sites.text: Early Sikh settlers arrived around 1904.

sites.name: Mombasa
sites.text: Start of the Uganda Railway, built partly by Punjabi workers.

steps.title: Partition of the Punjab
steps.text: The partition of India divided the Punjab, and almost all Sikhs in the new Pakistan fled east amid terrible violence. Many holy sites, including Nanak's birthplace, were left across the border.

sites.name: Wagah
sites.text: The border crossing between Lahore and Amritsar.

steps.label: 1984 to today
steps.title: Crisis and a global community
steps.text: The army's assault on the Golden Temple in 1984 and the killing of thousands of Sikhs in Delhi after Indira Gandhi's assassination left deep scars. Today about 25 million Sikhs live worldwide, with large communities in Britain, Canada, the United States and Australia.

sites.name: Amritsar
sites.text: Site of Operation Blue Star in June 1984.

sites.name: Kartarpur Corridor
sites.text: A visa-free route opened in 2019 for Indian pilgrims to visit Kartarpur.
